title: How does an Asian elephant use its trunk?
answer: An Asian elephant can pull a branch close, pick up a tiny object, and raise a load of water with the same tool: its trunk. A trunk is an extended nose and upper lip. It also smells with its trunk and reaches out with it to touch other elephants.

answer: A beaver can turn a shallow stream into a pond by piling branches and mud across it. Water slows down behind the dam and spreads into a wider area. That water helps a beaver move branches and swim safely to its home. A home built from sticks and mud is called a lodge. It can have an opening under the pond’s surface. answer: A giant panda spends much of its day finding and chewing bamboo. Its heavy jaws break tough stems, and a special wrist bone sticks out where a thumb might be. answer: A black-footed ferret may spend much of the day underground in tunnels dug by prairie dogs. answer: At some deep-sea vents, tiny living things can use energy from chemicals in the water to make food. They do not have to catch light from the Sun. This way of making food is called chemosynthesis. Giant tube worms can grow beside some of those vents. They have bacteria living inside them that make food, and the worms help bring the bacteria the chemicals they need. Other animals may eat bacteria or feed on animals that depend on them.
aliases: How can tube worms live in the dark ocean?
facts: Plants generally use light to make food, which is called photosynthesis.
Many other sea-floor animals still depend on bits of food falling from sunny waters.

questions.text: Where does hot, mineral-rich water come from under the sea?

title: How far does sunlight reach into the ocean?
answer: When you travel down through clear ocean water, the sunlight gets weaker. Near the top, enough light reaches plants and tiny algae for them to make food. Farther down, a dim band has traces of daylight, but too little for much food making by light. Deeper still, sunlight never reaches. Animals there can eat other animals or food that sinks down from above. Some can even make their own light while they move through the dark.
aliases: What are the sunlight and twilight zones?
Why is the deep ocean dark?
facts: In clear water, the sunlit upper zone can reach roughly 200 meters deep.
Deep water also presses harder on an animal than water near the surface.

questions.text: How does an animal make light where the Sun cannot reach?
How can food be made in complete darkness?
How deep do some narrow parts of the ocean floor reach?

title: How can an animal make its own light?
answer: Some living things can give off light by mixing chemicals inside their bodies. That light is called bioluminescence. A firefly uses flashes to signal to other fireflies. Some deep-sea fish use a shining spot to draw smaller animals closer. Other ocean animals can give off a flash when disturbed, which may distract a predator. Making a light is especially useful far below the ocean surface, where a tiny flash can stand out in the darkness.
aliases: Why do some sea animals glow?
facts: Much of the light made by ocean animals is blue or green.
A shiny object reflects light, but a bioluminescent animal makes light.

questions.text: Where does the ocean become completely dark?
What tiny ocean drifters might make a faint flash?

title: What makes a tsunami different from wind waves?
answer: A tsunami starts when a great amount of ocean water is suddenly pushed out of place. An earthquake that lifts or drops part of the ocean floor can start one. Far from land it can travel very quickly, while the surface may not look unusually high to someone on a boat. Near a coast, the water gets shallower and the waves slow and may grow taller. A tsunami can bring several surges, one after another.
aliases: Can an earthquake cause a huge wave?
facts: Underwater landslides can also start tsunamis.
An ordinary ocean wave usually begins when wind moves across the surface.

questions.text: How can a quake move solid ground suddenly?
How does wind make the waves seen on a normal beach?

title: Why can water rush away from a beach?
answer: As waves break near a beach, they push water toward land. Some of that water flows back out in a narrow, fast-moving stream called a rip current. A gap between sandbanks or a place next to a pier can give it a path. The stream pulls water away from shore, rather than sucking it straight down. Even when the beach looks calm, water can move quickly in one small part of the surf.
aliases: What is the difference between a rip and a tide?
facts: Rip currents can form on shores of large lakes as well as the ocean.
A rip current is a flow of water, rather than the rise and fall of a tide.

questions.text: How does water change as an ocean wave reaches a beach?
What causes seawater to rise and fall over hours?

title: Where is the deepest part of the ocean?
answer: The ocean floor is not flat. Long, narrow valleys called trenches cut deeply below nearby areas. The deepest known place is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean. It is about eleven kilometers below the surface. Many trenches form where one moving plate bends and slides beneath another. A person could not breathe or stand the pressure at that depth without a specially designed vessel to protect them.
facts: Sunlight does not reach the bottom of Earth’s deepest trenches.
The pressure at Challenger Deep is much greater than at the surface.

questions.text: Why can pieces of Earth’s outer layer move under each other?
How do light and pressure change as you go deeper?
What happens at a place where two plates move apart instead?

title: How does new seafloor form?
answer: Long chains of underwater mountains rise along parts of the ocean floor. Many form where two plates move apart. Hot rock rises under the gap, and some of it melts. Fresh material that reaches the surface cools and becomes part of the seafloor. As the plates keep moving, each new strip carries older rock farther from the middle. The ridge and its two sides keep a record of changes over immense stretches of time.
facts: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through much of the Atlantic Ocean.
Places called hydrothermal vents often form close to ridges.

questions.text: Why do the big pieces of Earth’s surface move at all?

title: What is a red tide?
answer: Tiny algae are a normal part of the ocean. When some kinds get conditions that help them grow very quickly, they can form a big patch called a bloom. Some blooms make chemicals that can hurt fish, other wildlife, or people. Those harmful blooms are sometimes called red tides, though the water can have other colors or look unchanged. Other algae blooms are harmless. Scientists test water to learn which kind is there.
aliases: What causes a harmful algal bloom?
Why does ocean water sometimes turn red?
facts: An algal bloom may be patchy and move with currents.
The term red tide does not mean that high or low tide has arrived.

questions.text: Which tiny creatures are ordinary members of ocean food webs?

title: How can hungry sea otters help a kelp forest?
answer: Sea otters float on their backs and can hold food above the water as they eat. Some use a stone to open a hard shell. Their diet can include crabs, clams, and sea urchins. An otter that eats urchins can reduce the number nibbling on kelp. Where that happens, kelp can grow thick enough for many other animals to shelter among its blades. An otter keeps warm with a dense coat that traps air next to its skin.
facts: Sea otters groom their coats to keep them working well.
In parts of the Pacific, sea otters are closely connected with kelp forest health.

questions.text: What kinds of animals can live under kelp?

title: How does an octopus fit into a narrow hole?
answer: A giant Pacific octopus has eight strong arms with suckers and a soft body. The hard beak in the center of its arms is one of the widest hard parts it must fit through an opening. It can squeeze into spaces that look too small for it at first. The octopus often hides among rocks on the floor of the northern Pacific Ocean. It can change color and make its skin look bumpier when it matches its surroundings.
aliases: How many arms does an octopus have?
facts: An octopus has arms with suckers along much of their length.
A mother octopus guards her eggs.

questions.text: Which octopus relative has a hard outside shell?

title: Why is a nautilus shell divided into rooms?
answer: A chambered nautilus is an ocean animal with a coiled shell divided by walls. Its soft body lives in the large room near the opening. Smaller rooms behind it contain gas and liquid. Changing the amount of liquid helps the animal stay at a useful depth without needing to swim all the time. A tube called a siphuncle connects its body to the rooms. The nautilus can pull much of its body into the outer room for protection.
facts: A nautilus is related to octopuses and squids.
It has many long tentacles, without suckers like an octopus’s.

questions.text: How can a relative that lacks a hard shell squeeze into openings?
Why can a gas-filled chamber change how something floats?

title: What were the three horns of Triceratops for?
answer: Triceratops walked on four legs and ate plants. Two long horns rose above its eyes, and it had a smaller horn over its nose. A bony frill spread out from the back of its skull. The horns and frill could have been useful for protection, display, or contests with other Triceratops. Scientists look at skulls for signs of damage and at how these structures changed as the animal grew to learn how it might have used them.
facts: Triceratops had a hard beak at the front of its mouth.
It lived in western North America toward the end of the age of most dinosaurs.

questions.text: How does a smaller dinosaur with a frill differ from Triceratops?

title: Why did Stegosaurus have plates down its back?
answer: Two rows of tall plates stood along the back of Stegosaurus. The plates were made of bone, but sat in the skin rather than joining the backbone. They could have made the animal look bigger or helped other stegosauruses see it. Scientists are still working out their uses. Four pointed spikes near the end of the tail were different. The animal could swing its tail, so these spikes may have helped defend it against a predator.
aliases: What dinosaur had tall plates and tail spikes?
facts: Stegosaurus ate plants and walked on four legs.
Its head was small compared with the rest of its body.

questions.text: Which other dinosaur had a heavy club at the end of its tail?

title: How was Ankylosaurus armored?
answer: Ankylosaurus was a low, wide dinosaur that ate plants. Like the hard covering on a turtle, rows of bony plates helped protect it. Its plates were set into skin across much of its back and neck. Its tail ended in a large lump of bone that could have worked like a club. A powerful swing might have made it difficult for a hunter to get near. An opening at the front of its jaws formed a beak for cropping leaves.
aliases: Dinosaur with a ball on its tail
What did Ankylosaurus use its tail for?
facts: Ankylosaurus supported its heavy body on four legs.
The tail club was not one single round bone.

questions.text: How was a tail with spikes different from a tail club?

title: Why did Diplodocus have such a long tail?
answer: Diplodocus was a long-necked dinosaur with a tail that narrowed to a thin tip. The tail alone made up a large part of its length. It may have helped the animal balance, send signals, or defend itself. Diplodocus gathered plant material with narrow teeth grouped near the front of its mouth. It did not have the broad grinding teeth people use to chew. Keeping its feet in one spot, it could reach plants over a wide area.
facts: Diplodocus walked on four legs and supported a long neck.
Fossils show that it lived in what is now western North America.

questions.text: How did another long-necked dinosaur reach higher plants?

title: How did Brachiosaurus reach high leaves?
answer: Brachiosaurus had long front legs that lifted its shoulders higher than its hips. From that sloping body, a long neck reached upward, so the animal could have gathered leaves well above the height most dinosaurs could reach. Its small head had teeth suited to taking pieces from plants. Even with an unusual shape, its four thick legs supported it on land. Its name means arm lizard because its front legs are such an obvious feature.
aliases: Which dinosaur had very long front legs?
facts: The known fossils come from the western United States.
Brachiosaurus belonged to the long-necked dinosaur group called sauropods.

title: How large was a real Velociraptor?
answer: Velociraptor was about as long as an adult human lying down, but much of that length was its tail. It was shorter and lighter than many movie raptors. A curved claw on the second toe of each foot could help it hold small prey. Marks on a fossil forearm are evidence that feathers grew there. Velociraptor ran on two legs and lived in what is now central Asia, where fossils preserve one caught alongside a Protoceratops.
facts: On each back foot, one large curved claw stood out.
A famous fossil shows Velociraptor and Protoceratops together.

title: Why did Iguanodon have a spike on its thumb?
answer: One finger on an Iguanodon hand ended in an unusual spike. Some early researchers put the spike on the dinosaur’s nose because they had only scattered fossils to work with. More complete hands showed where it belonged. The spike may have helped with defense. Iguanodon gathered plants with its beak and used rows of teeth farther back to cut plant material. It could move on two legs or on all fours.
facts: Iguanodon’s name refers to the shape of its teeth.

title: What is the tall sail on a Spinosaurus?
answer: Spinosaurus had very tall bones projecting from its spine. Together they supported a sail-like rise above its back. Its jaws were long, with pointed teeth shaped a little like cones, which fit well for catching slippery food like fish. Fossils suggest it spent time around water, but scientists still discuss exactly how it moved and hunted there. Spinosaurus lived in northern Africa at a time when large river systems covered places that are much drier today.
facts: Some Spinosaurus fossils were discovered in Egypt and Morocco.
Spinosaurus teeth have a different shape from the cutting teeth of many large hunters.

title: What could a Parasaurolophus crest do?
answer: Parasaurolophus had a long hollow crest that swept back from the top of its head. The crest contained connected passages from its nose. Air moving through the passages might have changed the sound the animal could make, somewhat like the way a long musical instrument can change a note. The crest also shaped its outline and may have helped other dinosaurs recognize it. A beak and rows of teeth let Parasaurolophus gather and chew plants.

facts: Parasaurolophus could move on two feet or all four.

title: How did Allosaurus bite its food?
answer: Allosaurus was a big predator during the Jurassic Period. Its teeth curved backward and had tiny notches along the edges. The teeth could grip pieces of food while the edges helped cut through them. Short ridges of bone stood above the eyes. Allosaurus walked on powerful back legs, with its tail stretched behind it. It lived alongside large plant eaters, including Stegosaurus. Fossil skeletons and bite marks are among the clues that help scientists work out what it ate.
facts: Many Allosaurus fossils have been found in the western United States.
Allosaurus did not live at the same time as Tyrannosaurus rex.

title: Why does Archaeopteryx look like both a bird and a dinosaur?
answer: An Archaeopteryx fossil can show feather marks beside the bones. The long feathers on the wings look much like some bird feathers today. The animal also had teeth, claws on its wings, and a long tail made of bone. These are features found in earlier dinosaurs related to birds. The mix of old and new features helped scientists understand how birds fit into the dinosaur family. Fossils from fine limestone in Germany preserve the outline of many of its feathers.
aliases: Ancient bird with teeth and feathers
facts: Archaeopteryx was about the size of a modern raven, depending on the specimen.
Its fossil specimens are from the Late Jurassic.

title: What was the thick dome on Pachycephalosaurus?
answer: Pachycephalosaurus walked on two legs and had an unusually thick dome of bone on top of its skull. Smaller bony bumps surrounded part of the head. The dome might have helped the animals push or bump each other during contests, or it might have made them easier to recognize. Scientists compare several kinds of evidence before choosing among these ideas. Many of the fossils found are fragments of skull, telling much more about the head than the rest of the animal.
aliases: Which dinosaur had a dome-shaped skull?
facts: Pachycephalosaurus means thick-headed lizard.
Its skull dome was solid bone.

title: What did Protoceratops look like?
answer: Protoceratops was a compact plant-eating dinosaur with a beak and a wide frill at the back of its head. It did not have the long horns of the later Triceratops. Scientists have found many Protoceratops fossils in rocks from Asia, including some belonging to young animals. One famous find held a Protoceratops near the bones of a Velociraptor, with the two bodies close together. That fossil provides an unusual clue about how dinosaurs sometimes met.
facts: Protoceratops was much smaller than Triceratops.

title: Why is Deinonychus called a terrible claw?
answer: Deinonychus had a large, sharply curved claw on one toe of each foot. Its name means terrible claw. The rest of its body included long arms and a tail that could help keep it balanced when it moved. Studying this dinosaur helped researchers rethink the idea that all dinosaurs were slow. Its bones suggested an active animal that could run on two feet. Deinonychus was related to Velociraptor, but its body was longer and heavier.
aliases: What was the larger cousin of Velociraptor?
facts: Deinonychus fossils have been found in North America.
Its back teeth curved backward.

title: Was Oviraptor really an egg thief?
answer: When an Oviraptor skeleton was found on a nest, researchers first thought the animal had been trying to eat another dinosaur’s eggs. Its name means egg thief. Years later, a fossil baby inside a matching kind of egg showed that eggs of that shape belonged to an Oviraptor relative. The adult on the nest may have been guarding or warming eggs. One new clue can change a good story about the past without requiring a change to the name.

facts: Oviraptor walked on two legs and had a beak.

title: What did an early little dinosaur look like?
answer: Coelophysis was a lightly built dinosaur with a long neck and tail and small, sharp teeth. It walked and ran on its hind legs. Its legs were slender, giving it a very different shape from the huge four-legged plant eaters that appeared later. It lived during the Triassic Period, early in the age of dinosaurs. A fossil site in New Mexico holds the remains of many Coelophysis individuals in the same area, allowing researchers to compare their sizes and bones.

facts: The name Coelophysis refers to its hollow bones.

title: What helped woolly mammoths live in the cold?
answer: A woolly mammoth had a shaggy coat over much of its body. Smaller ears than many living elephants also helped reduce heat loss. Its long, curved tusks could have helped push snow aside to reach plants, among other uses. Woolly mammoths lived much later than most dinosaurs. Some bodies froze in cold ground and kept their hair, skin, or stomach contents. Those finds give clues a normal fossil made only of bone cannot provide.
facts: Some woolly mammoth remains have been preserved in Alaska and Siberia.
Mammoths and modern elephants are relatives.

title: Were pterosaurs flying dinosaurs?
answer: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles that lived while many dinosaurs walked on land. Their wings stretched between their bodies and one very long finger on each hand. They had no feathered wing like a bird. Some were small and probably ate insects, while others reached the length of a small aircraft from wingtip to wingtip. Fossil wings and footprints show that some pterosaurs also walked on four limbs when they were on the ground.
facts: Pterosaurs belonged to a separate branch from dinosaurs.
They were the first known animals with backbones to achieve powered flight.

title: What was a trilobite?
answer: A trilobite was a small ocean animal related to today’s insects, spiders, and crabs. Its outer shell was divided along its length into a center section and two side sections. The three parts give trilobites their name. Many had eyes and short legs underneath, though the soft parts are much harder to find in fossils. As a trilobite grew, it sometimes left its old shell behind. Trilobites lived for a span of time much longer than dinosaurs later did.
facts: Trilobites lived in ancient seas.
Some trilobites could roll into a ball.

title: What lived inside an ammonite shell?
answer: Many ammonites left fossils that look like stone spirals. In life, an ammonite was a sea animal related to squids and octopuses, and the shell held its soft body. As it grew, it added new parts to the shell, sealing off older rooms behind it. Ammonites evolved many different shell shapes. Their fossils help researchers compare the ages of rocks, since some distinct kinds were common for only a short part of Earth’s past.
facts: Ammonites lived in the ocean.
Many shells were coiled, but some ammonites had straighter or oddly curved shells.

title: How can an animal leave a fossil without leaving a bone?
answer: A track in soft mud can fill in with sand. Later, the mud and sand can harden into rock. When some of that rock breaks away, it may reveal an imprint or a raised copy of the track. A trace fossil records something an animal did instead of preserving its body. Tracks can show how many feet used to touch the ground, how big they were, and whether more than one animal walked through the same place.
facts: Burrows, feeding marks, and footprints can all be trace fossils.
A row of related footprints is called a trackway.

title: What can fossil poop tell us?
answer: A coprolite is a dropping that became a fossil. While an animal’s body tells us what the animal looked like, what it left behind may tell us something about how it lived. A researcher might find a fish scale, a piece of bone, or a bit of plant trapped inside. Those pieces are clues to what the animal ate. Since different animals may leave similar droppings, figuring out which one made a fossil can be much harder.
aliases: How do scientists use fossil poop?
facts: A coprolite is a kind of trace fossil.
Some fossil droppings preserve tiny fragments that are easier to see under a microscope.

title: How can a whole river of ice move?
answer: When more snow falls each year than melts, layers can build up. The weight presses the snow below into dense ice. When the mass becomes thick enough, gravity pulls it slowly downhill or outward. A moving mass of this kind is a glacier. It can bend and flow slowly even though it is solid. Rocks carried along the bottom may scrape and wear away the ground as the glacier moves.
facts: Glaciers may move while the air around them is below freezing.

title: What are the rocky ridges left by glaciers?
answer: A glacier can carry pebbles, boulders, and sand in or on the ice. When its edge melts, the rock may stay behind, making a ridge called a moraine. A ridge along the side shows part of a glacier’s former edge. A stripe of rock in the middle of a glacier can form where two streams of ice join and bring their rocky sides together. These ridges can last long after the ice is gone.
facts: A moraine can hold rocks of many sizes mixed together.

title: Why is a glacial valley shaped like a U?
answer: A river often cuts a narrow trench with sloping sides. A glacier can fill much more of that valley and rub against its bottom and sides. It can carve a broad floor and high walls. When the ice retreats, the valley may look like a U in a view from one end. A smaller glacier nearby can cut a shallower valley that ends high above the floor of the main valley.
facts: A fjord is a glacial valley flooded by seawater.
Some waterfalls pour out of side valleys.

questions.text: How can a river do a different kind of carving?
What rocky piles can be left when the ice retreats?

title: How can a river carve a deep canyon?
answer: Water carrying sand and stones can wear away the bottom of a riverbed. Over a very long time a river may cut much deeper into the land. Rain, falling rocks, and side streams can wear away its sides. In a deep canyon, different layers of rock may show on the walls. Some form cliffs because they are harder to wear away. Other layers form slopes as pieces of rock break down.
aliases: How did running water shape the Grand Canyon?
facts: The Colorado River runs through the Grand Canyon.

questions.text: How does a valley carved by ice look different?

title: How does a hole become a natural rock arch?
answer: In places such as Arches National Park, cracks split sandstone into long, narrow walls. Rain can get into cracks, and pieces of rock gradually break and fall away. Sometimes a weak part low on a wall disappears before the stone above it. If the stone overhead still joins both sides, it can stand as an arch. The rock keeps wearing away after an arch forms. An arch can collapse when it gets too weak.
aliases: Why can a rock arch stand up?
facts: Many rock walls at Arches National Park are called fins.

questions.text: How does a different shape form when a top layer wears down more slowly?
How does loose sand turn into rock in the first place?

title: How does erosion leave a narrow tower of stone?
answer: A hoodoo is a tall, narrow shape made by rock wearing away unevenly. At Bryce Canyon, water enters cracks and can freeze when it gets cold. Ice takes more room than liquid water and pushes cracks wider. Repeated freezing and thawing loosen pieces from a wall until parts can stand alone. A harder top layer can protect softer rock beneath it for a while. The tower’s sides are still being worn away.
aliases: How did Bryce Canyon hoodoos form?
facts: Rain can slowly dissolve part of the rock at Bryce Canyon.

questions.text: What can happen when a gap opens through a narrow wall?

title: How can there be water beneath the ground?
answer: Some rain soaks through soil into openings between grains or into cracks in rock. If enough of those openings connect, water can move through them. A layer that stores water and lets enough pass through it to supply a well is called an aquifer. Water can come out again at a spring or enter a stream from below. Most underground water is in gaps rather than in one big open lake.
aliases: Where does well water come from?
facts: The top of the saturated zone is often called the water table.

questions.text: What happens when underground water finds a path back to the surface?

title: Why can water flow straight out of a hillside?
answer: A spring is a place where underground water reaches the surface. Rain or melted snow can sink through gaps in soil and rock. Water may collect above a layer that is slow to let it through. It moves along openings until those openings reach a stream bank, a hillside, or the bottom of a valley. That water can make a creek even when no rain is falling right above it.
aliases: Where does spring water come from?
facts: Some springs shrink or stop during a long dry period.

questions.text: How is water stored in rock and soil below our feet?

How does fresh water flow together after it reaches a stream?

title: Why can the ground suddenly sink into a hole?
answer: Rainwater can slowly dissolve some kinds of rock underground, including limestone. The openings can grow as more water passes through. Sometimes soil slips into the opening a little at a time, leaving a shallow bowl on the surface. In other places a roof of soil holds up for a while and then drops, opening a deeper hole more quickly. Not every sinkhole happens in the same way.
facts: Sinkholes can form by gradual sinking or sudden collapse.

title: Which cave formations hang down and which grow up?
answer: Water can pass through rock and carry dissolved material into a cave. As a drop hangs from the ceiling, it may leave a little solid mineral. The next drop can leave a little more. A formation hanging downward is a stalactite. Drops that hit the floor can add to a mound called a stalagmite. If both grow far enough, they can form a column from floor to ceiling.

How do cave icicle shapes form?
facts: Some cave formations grow extremely slowly.

title: How can things that lived in the sea become limestone?
answer: Some limestone begins with bits of shells and other hard parts from life in water. The bits settle to the bottom and build layers. Material left between the pieces helps bind them into rock. Limestone can also form when dissolved minerals come out of water without shells. Much of it is rich in calcium carbonate. Water with a little natural acid can dissolve limestone slowly, giving some caves space to grow.
aliases: Why do caves often form in limestone?
facts: Many fossils are found in limestone.

title: How can mud, sand, or shells become rock?
answer: Sand, mud, and pieces of shells can settle when moving water or air slows down. A new layer may cover an older one. With enough layers, the weight above can squeeze grains together. Material left behind by water passing between them can act like glue. Over time, many loose grains become a solid sedimentary rock. Some kinds form directly from material dissolved in water rather than from separate pieces.
facts: Sandstone contains sand-sized grains.

title: What happens when melted rock cools?
answer: Melted rock below the ground is called magma. If it reaches the surface, it is called lava. As either one cools and becomes solid, it forms igneous rock. Where magma cools slowly underground, grains of different minerals have more time to grow. A thin flow at the surface can cool quickly and have grains too small to see. Some kinds of melted rock become glass instead of forming many crystals.
aliases: What is the difference between intrusive and extrusive rock?
facts: Granite is an igneous rock that forms underground.

title: How can a solid rock change without melting?
answer: A rock buried deep underground can warm up and be squeezed hard. Minerals may change shape or grow again, and new minerals may appear. The rock can change its pattern and strength while staying mostly solid. A rock changed this way is called metamorphic. Slate can come from a kind of muddy rock, and marble can come from limestone. A piece can keep clues about the rock it once was.
aliases: Where do slate and marble come from?
facts: Some metamorphic rocks split along flat layers.

title: Why can you see several colors in one piece of granite?
answer: A polished piece of granite can show pink, white, gray, or dark grains that fit together. The grains are different minerals. They grew when melted rock cooled slowly underground. Slow cooling gave the minerals time to form pieces big enough to see. Granite may only become visible long after it cools, when the rock above it wears away. A cut countertop can reveal some of the same patterns as a boulder outdoors.
facts: Quartz and feldspar are common in granite.

title: Why does some volcanic rock look like glass?
answer: Obsidian is a natural glass that can form when some kinds of lava cool quickly. The material becomes solid before crystals have time to grow very much. The surface can be shiny. A break often leaves a curved hollow that looks a bit like the inside of a shell. People in different parts of the world once used pieces of obsidian as cutting tools because a broken edge can be quite sharp.
facts: Many pieces of obsidian are dark, but the color can vary.

title: How can a rock float?
answer: Pumice forms when particular kinds of melted rock have gas bubbles in them as they cool. After the rock hardens, it is full of holes where bubbles used to be. A piece of pumice can look solid from far away, but much of its inside may be empty space. That makes some pieces less dense than water, so they float. Water may later soak into the holes and change whether a piece floats.
aliases: Why does pumice have so many holes?
facts: Pumice is volcanic rock.

title: Why are some volcanic islands lined up?
answer: A hot spot can supply melted rock beneath a moving plate. A volcano may grow above the hot spot until it reaches the ocean surface and makes an island. The plate then carries the island farther along. A new volcano can form nearer the hot spot. Over a long time, this can leave a chain with younger volcanoes toward one end and older ones toward the other. The Hawaiian chain records this pattern.

Why do some Hawaiian islands have older rocks?
facts: A hot spot can supply volcanoes far from a plate edge.

title: Why does a geyser erupt over and over?
answer: A geyser has a narrow or twisted route below ground to water heated by nearby hot rocks. Water deeper down can become very hot under the weight of water above it. As some water turns to steam and pushes water out, the pressure deep down drops. More steam forms quickly and the geyser sprays hot water. After the burst, water can seep back into the openings so the process begins again.
aliases: What makes geysers different from hot springs?
facts: Most hot springs lack the kind of plumbing that lets a geyser erupt.

title: How can a hill decide which river gets the rain?
answer: A watershed is an area where water drains toward the same river, lake, or other low place. Rain falling on opposite sides of a ridge may reach different streams. A stream’s small watershed can fit inside a bigger one if the stream flows into a river. Water can take different routes along the surface or partly underground. Drawing the high ground around a river helps to map the land that sends water toward it.
facts: A watershed boundary often follows high ground.

title: How does wind build a hill out of sand?
answer: Wind can bounce small sand grains along the ground. If the wind slows near a plant, rock, or other obstacle, loose grains can pile up. On many dunes, sand climbs the gentler side facing the wind. It spills over the top and slides down the steeper side. Repeating this can move a dune little by little, even though each grain travels only a short way. Changes in wind can change the dune’s shape.
aliases: Why is one side of a dune steep?
facts: Dunes can form inland as well as near beaches.

title: Why does a river sometimes spread into nearby land?
answer: Water reaches a river from streams, slopes, rain, and melting snow. If water comes in faster than it can flow away, the river rises. It may spill onto nearby flat land, called a floodplain. When water spreading there slows, some mud and sand can settle out. Over many floods, this can add material to the land near a river. During lower water, rivers may return to a smaller, deeper channel.

facts: Snowmelt and heavy rain can contribute to floods.

title: Why do snowflakes usually have six sides?
answer: A snowflake begins when water forms a tiny ice crystal in a cold cloud. Water molecules fit together in a repeating pattern in ice. The pattern usually gives this kind of crystal six sides or six main branches. As the crystal drifts through the cloud, it can grow new parts. The air’s temperature and moisture affect how it grows. Some crystals look like stars, while others look more like plates, needles, or short columns.
aliases: Why do snowflakes have six points?
facts: Snow can include crystals stuck together.

title: How does a summer thunderstorm make ice?
answer: A thunderstorm can send a strong stream of air upward. Water droplets often stay liquid even when they are below their usual freezing temperature. When some strike a piece of ice, they can freeze onto it. The growing lump gets heavier as it picks up more. A hailstone falls when the rising air can no longer keep it up or when the wind carries it out into air that is not rising as quickly.

facts: A hailstone can show several layers of ice.

title: How can a snowflake turn into an ice pellet?
answer: Snow may start falling through air cold enough to keep it frozen. Sometimes a layer of warmer air farther down partly melts the flakes. If they then fall through a deep enough layer of below-freezing air close to the ground, they freeze again. They reach the ground as ice pellets. Those pellets may bounce when they hit a hard surface, in contrast to a snowflake that lands softly or a raindrop that splashes.
facts: In weather reports in the United States, sleet means ice pellets.

title: Why can falling rain turn to ice on a branch?
answer: Freezing rain begins with liquid drops. Those drops can cool below water’s usual freezing point without turning solid right away. If they reach a surface that is at or below freezing, such as a road or a wire, they can freeze when they land. Drop after drop leaves a coating of ice. Sleet forms in a different way because the drops freeze into pellets before striking anything on the ground.

title: How can a lake make extra snow?
answer: Cold air blowing over a stretch of unfrozen lake picks up heat and water vapor from the water. The warmed, moister air rises and cools. Some of its water forms clouds and then snow. Winds usually carry the clouds toward the far shore of the lake. A narrow area can get much more snow than another place a short drive away, depending on where the wind carries the cloud bands.

facts: Lake-effect snow happens near the Great Lakes and can happen near some other lakes too.

title: Is ground fog really a cloud?
answer: Fog is a cloud close enough to the ground for people to walk through it. On a quiet, clear night, the ground can lose heat. Air touching it cools too. When the air cools enough, some of its invisible water vapor forms tiny liquid drops. Many suspended drops make it harder to see through the air. After sunlight warms the ground and the air again, the drops may evaporate and the fog can thin out.
facts: Fog droplets usually stay in the air rather than falling like rain.

title: Why is grass wet on a morning when it did not rain?
answer: After sunset, a blade of grass can cool more quickly than the air a little above it. Air touching the blade also cools. If it cools enough, some of the water vapor in that air turns into tiny liquid drops on the grass. That water is dew. Dew can also appear on a car, a spider web, or a picnic table. A glass of cold water can gain drops on the outside by the same general process.
facts: Dew forms at a surface, while fog droplets hang in the air.

title: How do ice crystals grow on a window?
answer: Frost can form when moist air touches a surface that is cold enough for water to turn directly from vapor into ice. The new ice can grow in delicate branches across a window or along a blade of grass. An object outdoors may cool below freezing even if the air a few feet above it is a little warmer. Frost is different from a layer left by rain that lands and then freezes.

title: What is the jet stream?
answer: High above the ground, there are narrow bands of fast wind called jet streams. They often form near places where there is a large difference in temperature between masses of air. The bands bend and take different routes as the air moves. When jets shift, they can steer some storms along new paths. Airplanes can gain time when they fly in the same direction as a jet stream, because the moving air helps carry them.

title: What happens when two kinds of air meet?
answer: A weather front is where a mass of colder air and a mass of warmer air meet. In a cold front, advancing cold air often slides under warm air, which can make the warm air rise quickly. In a warm front, advancing warm air can glide up over colder air close to the ground. Rising air usually cools, allowing clouds and sometimes precipitation to form. If the meeting place barely moves, the weather may linger.

facts: Fronts may bring changes in wind, temperature, and sky cover.

title: What can you tell from the shape of a cloud?
answer: Gray clouds that spread like a blanket are often stratus clouds. Cumulus clouds can grow in white heaps as air rises in separate columns. Cirrus clouds are usually high, cold, and thin, with streaks that look like wisps of hair. A cloud’s height and shape give clues about the air where it grew. Those clues become more useful when you look at many clouds moving and changing instead of just one cloud for a moment.

facts: Many high cirrus clouds are made mainly of ice crystals.

title: What makes the wind blow?
answer: Air pushes on things even when it looks empty. When air pushes more strongly in one place than in a nearby place, it starts moving from the higher pressure toward lower pressure. Uneven warming of the land and sea can help make pressure differences. Once air moves, the spin of Earth can bend its path over large distances. Buildings, hills, and trees can slow wind or change its direction close to the ground.
aliases: What is the cause of wind?
facts: A stronger difference in pressure over a short distance can produce stronger wind.

title: How can invisible air press on things?
answer: Air is made of moving molecules that bump into your skin and other surfaces all the time. Those tiny pushes add up to air pressure. Near sea level, a lot of air lies above you, pressing down on the air below. At the top of a tall mountain, less air rests above you. The pressure is generally lower there. When air pressure changes from place to place, air can start moving as wind.

title: Is sea ice made from seawater?
answer: Sea ice starts when ocean water becomes cold enough to freeze. Salt makes seawater freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water. As ice forms, much of the salt stays in the water below or gets trapped in small pockets. Winds and currents can pile pieces together or push them apart. A very different kind of floating ice arrives when part of a glacier breaks off the land and drifts away as an iceberg.

facts: Sea ice comes from the ocean surface freezing.

title: Why is most of an iceberg under water?
answer: Icebergs form when pieces break off a glacier or a floating extension of one. An iceberg’s ice is usually made from snow that fell on land, so it is mostly fresh water. Ice is less dense than the water it floats in. Even so, most of a floating iceberg sits underwater, with a smaller share showing above the surface. The hidden part can stretch well beyond the edges a person sees from a boat.

title: When does a new plant or animal become invasive?
answer: Some living things reach new places when people carry boats, plants, soil, or other goods between regions. Some newcomers never establish a wild population. Some live in their new place without harming it. One is considered invasive if it spreads outside its native range and causes harm. For example, a fast-growing plant could crowd out other plants that local insects need. A new animal might eat food that another species depends on. Scientists look for actual harm, rather than judging a kind of life just because it came from somewhere else.
facts: A species can cause problems in one area and be useful in its native habitat.

title: Why would people build a bridge for animals?
answer: A road can cut between places where animals eat, drink, or raise young. A bridge covered with soil and plants can let some animals cross above moving cars. Others use a passage below the pavement. Fences can keep animals from trying to enter the road and guide them to a crossing. People choose locations by finding existing animal travel routes. A crossing can help keep part of a larger habitat connected.

title: How can a pile of oysters become a reef again?
answer: An oyster can attach to a hard object. If many oysters grow next to and on top of one another, their shells form a rough structure with cracks and ledges. Small animals can hide there. Oysters also filter tiny pieces of food from water as they feed. Where older reefs have disappeared, groups can restore them by providing clean shells or another firm base for young oysters to attach to and grow.

title: How can a fire change which plants grow in a forest?
answer: Fire may harm trees and animals, but some ecosystems developed with fires from time to time. In some forests, fires remove low plants that compete for sunlight. Heat can open some kinds of tightly closed cones, releasing seeds. Plants may also sprout again from roots that survived below ground. An unusually severe fire can leave very different effects than a mild one, so what grows back depends on the place and the fire.

title: How can an animal return to a place where it disappeared?
answer: A species may disappear from one place while still living somewhere else. Reintroduction means bringing some back to a suitable place in its former range. Before releasing animals, teams study threats, food, shelter, and other wildlife already there. A very rare species may need young raised in a protected setting. After release, people check whether the animals survive, find food, and have young. The hope is for a wild group that can continue on its own.

title: What does it mean when a species is endangered?
answer: An endangered species is one that is in danger of disappearing. If the last living member is gone, the species is extinct. A species can be in trouble because it has little habitat left, because there are too few young growing up, or because changing conditions make it harder to find food. Scientists look at where a species lives, how many are there, and whether groups are getting smaller. Those clues can help people decide how to protect it.

facts: A kind of animal can disappear from one region and still be alive somewhere else.

title: Why do monarch butterflies fly south in autumn?
answer: Many monarchs from eastern parts of North America head south in autumn. They gather in cool mountain forests in central Mexico, where the winter usually lets them survive without laying many eggs. When weather warms, they fly north and begin laying eggs. Later generations continue the journey. A female monarch looks for milkweed for its young, because monarch caterpillars eat milkweed leaves. Adult butterflies visit flowers for nectar and can use many different kinds.

title: Why did wolves return to Yellowstone?
answer: Gray wolves once lived in Yellowstone, but people removed them from the park and few remained nearby. In the 1990s, wildlife workers brought wolves from Canada back to the area. Wolves can hunt animals such as elk, which in turn feed on leaves and other plants. Animals can act differently when a predator returns. Scientists still compare the effects of wolves with other changes, including weather, food, and the actions of people.
